segments.text: Elements, Book three, Proposition thirty-five. If two chords intersect inside a circle, the rectangle contained by the segments of one chord equals the rectangle contained by the segments of the other. In circle A B C D, let chords A C and B D intersect at point E. We claim that the rectangle A E by E C equals the rectangle D E by E B. If both chords pass through the center E, all four segments A E, E C, D E, and E B are equal radii, so the rectangles contained by them are immediately equal.

segments.text: Because F G passes through the center perpendicular to chord A C, it bisects A C at G. Since A C is cut equally at G and unequally at E, Book two Proposition five shows that the rectangle A E by E C plus the square on E G equals the square on G C. Adding the square on F G to both sides, the Pythagorean theorem on right triangles F G E and F G C turns those sums into the square on F E and the square on radius F C. By the exact same reasoning on chord B D, the rectangle D E by E B plus the square on F E equals the square on radius F B. Since radii F C and F B have equal squares, subtracting the common square on F E leaves the rectangle A E by E C equal to the rectangle D E by E B, as was required to prove.

segments.text: Euclid proves four cases depending on whether one or neither chord passes through the center, while Campanus condensed the proof into this single general case. Together with Proposition thirty-six, it establishes the interior Power of a Point theorem: for any point E inside a circle of radius R at distance d from the center, the product of the chord segments through E is always R squared minus d squared. In the GEOMETOR dependency graph, Proposition thirty-five synthesizes fifty-seven ancestor nodes across Books one, two, and three—combining chord bisection from Book three Proposition three, the difference-of-squares rectangle identity from Book two Proposition five, and the Pythagorean theorem from Book one Proposition forty-seven.
